setup.zh: 出村时，吴婆婆把一块磨亮的木牌塞给你：「到了碑那儿，看看碑背面。」前山满地狗爪印——马家的围猎篦空了它。
setup.en: Leaving the village, Granny Wu pressed a worn token into your hand: "When you reach the stele, look at its back." The front slopes are all dog tracks — the Mas' hunts combed them bare.

recap.zh: 吴婆婆给了你一块狐纹木牌；前山被马家的围猎篦空了，只打着一只山鸡，马家的狗还追着要。
recap.en: Granny Wu gave you a fox-carved token; the Mas' hunts had combed the front slopes bare — one pheasant all morning, and the Mas' dogs came after that too.

zh: 村东头，瞎眼的吴婆婆，像在等你们。
一块磨得发亮的小木牌。
前山：满地狗爪印，马蹄印。
en: At the east end, blind Granny Wu, as if she were waiting.
A little wooden token, worn bright.
The front slopes: dog tracks and hoofprints everywhere.

text.zh: 木牌磨得发亮，刻着一只蜷着的狐狸，尾巴一圈圈绕着身子；揣在怀里，温温的。
text.en: The token is rubbed smooth: a curled fox, its tails wound round and round its body. Tucked inside your coat, it is warm.

text.zh: 狗爪印、马蹄印一层叠着一层，连兔子洞都给刨开了——马家篦过的山，连根兔毛都不剩。
text.en: Dog prints and hoofprints lie layer on layer; even the rabbit holes are dug open. Where the Mas have combed a hill, not a rabbit hair is left.

story.zh:
出村要经过村东头。井台边蹲着一个半大孩子，正在收麻雀网，瞧见爷儿俩背着弓往山里去，眼珠子转了一转。吴婆婆照旧坐在门槛上，一双白蒙蒙的眼睛朝着山的方向，倒像是专门在等他们。吴婆婆是石坳村最老的人，眼睛看不见，耳朵却比村里所有的狗加起来还灵。

谁家半夜偷了谁家的瓜，她第二天一早便知道，不但知道是谁偷的，还知道偷了几个，连哪个是生的都知道。

她问道：「去黑松岭？」小满他爹没吭声。

吴婆婆也不要他们回答，自顾自地道：「蒙山顶上从前住过一个骑白鹤的老头，一顿饭吃一颗枣，活了八百岁。」他爹道：「婆婆，我们赶路。」吴婆婆道：「嗯。他也赶路。」他爹便不再搭话，低头对小满道：「编的。」

吴婆婆摸索着从怀里掏出一样东西，塞进小满手里，却是一块小木牌，磨得发亮，上面刻着一只蜷着的狐狸。她道：「你爷爷走的那年，也从我这门口过。」

小满张了张嘴，一个字也没说出来。

吴婆婆又道：「到了碑那儿，看看碑背面。」小满问：「看什么？」吴婆婆笑了，露出仅剩的三颗牙，道：「看了，就知道了。不看，就不知道。」

小满觉得这句话说了跟没说一样，可还是把木牌揣进了怀里。他娘说过，老人家说话，十句里有九句是废话，剩下那一句，能救命。

小满他爹常说，打猎的人家有三样东西不能少：一张好弓，一双好腿，一副好耳朵。弓是小满爷爷传下来的，弓背裂过两回，拿牛筋缠着，远远看过去，像一条打了补丁的裤子。小满小时候问过一回，爷爷没回来，弓怎么回来的。

他爹只说了一句：「你爷爷没回来。弓回来了。」再问，便是「吃饭」。耳朵是他爹的，他能听见三里外一只獐子踩断一根枯枝。

至于腿，他爹的膝盖不行了，这两年，腿是小满的。

那一天，父子两个天没亮就进了山。前山什么也没有，满地都是狗爪印、马蹄印。原来马家入秋办了三场围猎，带着二十条猎狗、几十个家丁，把前山篦了一遍又一遍，篦得比他娘梳头还细。
story.en:
Leaving the village meant passing the east end. A half-grown boy crouched by the well, gathering in his sparrow nets; seeing father and son head for the hills with the bow, his eyes slid sideways. Granny Wu sat on her threshold as always, her clouded white eyes turned toward the mountain, as though she'd been waiting just for them. Granny Wu was the oldest person in Shi'ao Village; her eyes couldn't see, but her ears were sharper than every dog in the village put together.

If one family stole another's melons in the night she knew by morning — not only who, but how many, and even which ones were unripe.

She asked, "Black Pine Ridge?" Xiaoman's father said nothing.

Granny Wu didn't wait for an answer; she went on to herself: "On the top of Mount Meng there used to live an old man who rode a white crane. One jujube a meal, and he lived eight hundred years." His father said, "Granny, we've a road to walk." Granny Wu said, "Mm. So did he." His father answered no more, and said to Xiaoman under his breath, "Made up."

Granny Wu fumbled something out of her coat and pressed it into Xiaoman's hand: a little wooden token, rubbed to a shine, carved with a curled-up fox. She said, "The year your grandpa went, he passed this door too."

Xiaoman opened his mouth; not a word came out.

Granny Wu went on, "When you get to the stele, look at the back of it." Xiaoman asked, "Look at what?" Granny Wu laughed, showing her last three teeth. "Look, and you'll know. Don't look, and you won't."

Xiaoman felt the remark said about as much as nothing, but he tucked the token inside his jacket all the same. His mother had said: of ten things an old person says, nine are nonsense, and the one left over can save your life.

Xiaoman's father often said a hunting family can't do without three things: a good bow, a good pair of legs, a good pair of ears. The bow had come down from Xiaoman's grandfather; its back had split twice and was bound with ox sinew, and from a distance it looked like a pair of patched trousers. Once, when he was small, Xiaoman had asked how the bow came home when his grandfather didn't.

His father said only: "Your grandpa didn't come back. The bow did." Ask again, and it was "Eat your food." The ears were his father's: he could hear a river deer snap a dead twig three li away.

As for legs — his father's knee had given out, and these two years the legs were Xiaoman's.

That day father and son went into the mountains before dawn. The front hills held nothing — everywhere dog-paw prints, horse-hoof prints. The Ma family had held three hunts that autumn, with twenty hounds and dozens of servants, and combed the front hills over and over, combed them finer than his mother combed her hair.

label.en: Climb the tallest pine and look out

exits.means: climbs a tree to look out over the mountain, scouts, looks around

story.zh:
小满爬上最高的那棵松树，四下里望了半天，溜下来只说了一句：「爹。前山空了。」

他爹道：「空到什么地步？」小满道：「连耗子都搬家了。门口还贴了告示。」他爹道：「……写的什么？」小满道：「『马家在此，无鼠可活』。」他爹看了他一眼，瞧得出很想笑，但他忍住了，他的膝盖也忍住了。

前山既然空了，他爹便领着他往山里头走。走了一程，他爹忽然站住了，把背上那张弓解下来，拿在手里掂了一掂，道：「今儿教你一样东西。」小满登时来了精神。

那张弓在他爹手里使了几十年，小满摸过它的弓背，数过弓背上缠了几道牛筋，却从来没有拉过它，他爹不许。

他爹道：「这是你爷爷传下来的，叫《落雁三箭》。」小满道：「落雁？爹，你射下过大雁？」他爹道：「没有。」小满道：「那爷爷射下过？」

他爹想了一想，道：「也没有。你爷爷那年去镇上卖皮子，听说书先生讲什么『一箭落雁』，回来便给咱家这点本事起了个名儿。他说，起了名儿，就算武功了。」顿了一顿，又道：「那说书的还讲李广射石头，射进去了。你爷爷回来也射了一块。箭断了，一支箭，削一个晚上。」从那以后，沈家只射活的。

小满道：「那它到底是不是武功？」他爹道：「是三句话。一箭一句。你爷爷教我，一年只教一箭；我教你，也一年只教一箭。今年教头一箭。」说着把弓往地下一拄，一个字一个字地道：「**先看风，后看鹿。**」

小满等了一会儿，见他没有下文，问道：「……完了？」他爹道：「完了。」小满道：「就六个字？」他爹道：「你爷爷教我，也是六个字。」小满心想，一年六个字，照这么教将下去，等他学全了，他爹的膝盖只怕已经聊不动天了。

他爹不识字，他这一辈子没有一本书，他的书都在山里。他见儿子不服气，便蹲下来——蹲得极慢，左腿直直地伸着——拔了一根草，举到眼前，道：「你看。」只见那草尖儿微微地往东南歪。

他爹道：「风从西北来。你站在西北，鹿在东南，你还没瞧见它，它先闻见你了。风横着吹，箭出去便是歪的，你瞄得再准也没用。风一阵一阵的，你便等它歇一口气。」小满道：「那鹿呢？」他爹道：「风看明白了，鹿就跑不了。风看不明白，鹿就是别人的了。」

便在这时，他爹忽然伸手按住了他的肩膀，下巴往前一点。只见四十来步外一片乱草坡上，一只山鸡正低着头在草根里刨食，尾巴一翘一翘的，全然不知道这世上还有他们爷儿俩。他爹却不忙着拉弓，先看草。坡上的草一阵往这边倒，一阵又直起来。

他伸出一根指头，在嘴里含了一含，举在半空停了片刻，这才一声不响地往左边绕。

他那条左腿不利索，每一步都要先拿脚尖试一试地，一步，两步，足足绕了二十来步，绕到风正顺着他箭路吹的地方，背靠着一棵老栗子树站定——他那膝盖跪不得，只能站着射。然后他搭上箭，弓只开了一半，便那么端着。

小满屏住了气，等他拉弓，他却偏偏不拉。

一阵风从坡上刮过来，草尖一齐伏倒，他不动；风过去了，草尖晃了两晃，慢慢地直起来——便在草尖将直未直的那一霎，那张打了补丁的弓在他手里一气张满，弯得像一轮月牙儿，满了便放，只听得「嗖」的一声，那山鸡连扑腾都没来得及扑腾一下，已翻倒在草里。

一支箭，一只山鸡。小满奔过去把山鸡提起来，那一箭正穿在它的脖子上，不偏不倚。他爹接过箭来，先不看山鸡，拿袖子把箭头擦得干干净净，对着天光瞧了瞧箭杆直不直，这才插回箭壶里。

小满道：「爹，你箭都搭上了，还等什么？」他爹道：「等风歇一口气。」小满道：「风还会歇气？」他爹道：「什么东西都要歇气。风也是，鹿也是，人也是。」顿了一顿，又道：「马三也是。」这句话小满当时没听懂，可他觉得，这是他爹这辈子说过的最有学问的一句话，便牢牢地记住了。

还有一件事，他也记住了，只是没有说出口。昨天傍晚，他爹跪在马三跟前，两只手按在地下，是抖的；今天他爹拉开这张弓，两只手稳稳当当，连弓弦都没颤一颤。原来他爹这一双手，并不是天生会抖的。

小满道：「爹，那第二箭呢？」他爹道：「明年。」小满道：「先说个名儿听听。」他爹道：「名儿也是明年。」小满道：「那第三箭——」他爹道：「后年。」说了等于没说，小满觉得这一点，他爹倒有几分像吴婆婆。

小满不死心，心想弓拉不得，风总看得。走不多远，他学着他爹的样子，从头上拔下一根头发，捏着一头举在半空，要看它往哪边飘。那头发飘是飘了，却不往东，也不往西，一阵风过，直直地飘进了他爹嘴里。他爹「呸呸」吐了两口，回头看他。

小满道：「爹，风是往你那边吹的。」他爹道：「……我知道了。」

转到晌午，前山再没见着第二样活物。那只山鸡，便是爷儿俩一上午的全部收成，瘦得皮包骨，抱在怀里像抱着一把拖把。一只山鸡，抵不了一张鹿皮。他爹坐在一块石头上揉着膝盖，许久没有说话。

便在这时，山梁那边一阵狗叫，七八条黄狗冲下坡来，后头跟着两个马家的家丁，一个扛着叉，一个提着锣。跑在最前头领路的，却是老刘家的大小子刘豆芽，手里攥着半块桂花糕，一面跑，一面往嘴里塞。

扛叉的那个远远地便嚷：「站住！那只山鸡，姓马！」

小满认得那半块桂花糕。天没亮爷儿俩出村，除了村东头的吴婆婆，一路上只碰见过一个人，便是蹲在井台边收麻雀网的刘豆芽。马家的桂花糕是不白给的，这一趟前山，原来是拿半块糕换来的。

小满瞧了瞧怀里的山鸡，山鸡瘦得皮包骨，瞧不出姓什么。他爹拄着弓站起来，那条腿却迈不快。狗叫声越来越近。小满想起他娘的话：打不过就跑。可往回跑，是马家的狗；往两边跑，是马家的坡。只有一个方向，马家的狗是不去的。

他一把拽住他爹的胳膊，道：「爹，往里走。」

爷儿俩一瘸一拐，钻过一片荆棵子，那几条黄狗一路追到一块断碑跟前，忽然一齐刹住了脚，夹着尾巴，呜呜地叫，前爪在地上乱刨，就是不肯往前再迈一步。

提锣的那个家丁追上来，瞧见那块碑，脸也白了，拉住扛叉的道：「……算了，一只山鸡。」又压低了嗓子，「前几日那个穿白的老爷，赏了二两银子，问的就是这块碑。三爷都不让多嘴。」扛叉的瞪了他一眼，冲着林子嚷了一声：「三爷说了，立冬前黑松岭里射着的，也姓马！」两个人吆喝着狗，头也不回地走了。

刘豆芽落在最后，回头看了小满一眼，把剩下那口桂花糕咽了下去。
story.en:
Xiaoman climbed the tallest pine and looked all round for a long time, then slid down and said just one thing: "Dad. The front hills are empty."

His father said, "How empty?" Xiaoman said, "Even the rats have moved house. And put up a notice." His father said, "…Saying what?" Xiaoman said, "'The Mas are here — no rat survives.'" His father looked at him, plainly wanting very much to laugh; but he held it in, and so did his knee.

With the front hills empty, his father led him deeper in. After a stretch his father stopped, unslung the bow and weighed it in his hand. "Today I'll teach you something." Xiaoman perked up at once.

That bow had been in his father's hands for decades; Xiaoman had stroked its back and counted its sinew bindings, but never once drawn it. His father didn't allow it.

His father said, "Your grandpa handed this down. It's called *Three Arrows That Fell the Goose*." Xiaoman said, "Fell the goose? Dad, have you ever shot down a goose?" His father said, "No." "Then Grandpa did?"

His father thought. "No, not him either. The year your grandpa went to town to sell hides, he heard the storyteller going on about 'one arrow fells the goose', came home, and gave our bit of skill a name. He said once it had a name, it counted as a martial art." A pause. "That storyteller told of Li Guang shooting a rock, and the arrow going in. Your grandpa came home and shot one too. The arrow broke — one arrow, one night's whittling." Ever since, the Shens shot only living things.

Xiaoman said, "So is it a martial art or not?" His father said, "It's three sayings. One arrow, one saying. Your grandpa taught me one arrow a year; I'll teach you one arrow a year. This year, the first." He planted the bow on the ground and said, word by word: "**First read the wind, then the deer.**"

Xiaoman waited, and when nothing more came, asked, "…That's it?" His father said, "That's it." "Six words?" "Your grandpa taught me six words too." Xiaoman thought: six words a year — at that rate, by the time he'd learned it all, his father's knee would be too old to chat.

His father couldn't read; he'd never owned a book in his life; his books were all in the mountains. Seeing his son unconvinced, he crouched down — very slowly, his left leg stuck straight out — plucked a blade of grass and held it up. "Look." The tip leaned slightly southeast.

His father said, "Wind from the northwest. You stand northwest, the deer's southeast — before you've seen it, it's smelled you. A crosswind sends the arrow crooked; however well you aim, it's no use. When the wind comes in gusts, wait for it to catch its breath." Xiaoman said, "And the deer?" His father said, "Read the wind right, and the deer can't get away. Read it wrong, and the deer's someone else's."

Just then his father put a hand on his shoulder and jerked his chin forward. Forty-odd paces off, on a slope of rough grass, a pheasant had its head down scratching for food among the roots, tail flicking, with no idea there was a father and son in the world. His father didn't hurry to draw; he read the grass first. The grass on the slope bent this way in gusts, then stood up again.

He wet a finger in his mouth, held it up a moment, and only then circled left without a sound.

His left leg was bad; at every step he tested the ground with his toe first — one step, two — a good twenty paces round, until the wind ran straight along his line to the pheasant, and stood with his back to an old chestnut tree: that knee couldn't kneel, so he had to shoot standing.

Then he nocked an arrow, drew it halfway, and held it there. Xiaoman held his breath, waiting for him to draw; he didn't.

A gust came down the slope and the grass tips all bowed; he didn't move. The gust passed, the tips swayed twice and slowly straightened — and in the instant they were almost but not quite upright, his fingers opened. *Whoosh*: the pheasant hadn't even time to flap before it was over in the grass.

One arrow, one pheasant. Xiaoman ran and picked it up; the arrow had gone clean through its neck. His father took the arrow and, before looking at the bird, wiped the head spotless on his sleeve, sighted along the shaft against the sky to see it was straight, and only then put it back in the quiver.

Xiaoman said, "Dad, you had the arrow on the string — what were you waiting for?" His father said, "For the wind to catch its breath." Xiaoman said, "The wind catches its breath?" His father said, "Everything has to catch its breath. The wind does, the deer does, people do." A pause. "Ma San does." Xiaoman didn't understand that then, but he felt it was the most learned thing his father had ever said, and he fixed it firmly in his memory.

There was one more thing he fixed in his memory, only he didn't say it. Yesterday evening, kneeling before Ma San, his father's two hands pressed on the ground had been shaking; today, drawing this bow, his father's two hands were steady as rock, not even a tremor in the string. So his father's hands weren't born to shake after all.

Xiaoman said, "Dad, what about the second arrow?" His father said, "Next year." Xiaoman said, "Tell me its name at least." His father said, "The name's next year too." Xiaoman said, "Then the third —" His father said, "The year after." As good as saying nothing — in this, Xiaoman thought, his father was a bit like Granny Wu.

He hefted the pheasant, and a thought stirred. "Dad, let me try drawing it once." His father said, "No." Xiaoman said, "Just once." His father said, "You can't draw it. If you can't, you'll force it; if you force it, you'll hurt your hand; if you hurt your hand —" he glanced back at the bow on his back, "when Ma San comes, does he take the bow, or you?" Xiaoman thought about it, decided Ma San would probably take both, and didn't raise it again.

Xiaoman wouldn't give up: if he couldn't draw the bow, he could at least read the wind. Before long, copying his father, he plucked a hair from his head, held it up by one end to see which way it drifted. Drift it did — not east, not west: a breath of wind came and it floated straight into his father's mouth. His father spat twice, *pah, pah*, and looked round at him.

Xiaoman said, "Dad, the wind's blowing your way." His father said, "…I noticed."

By noon the front hills hadn't shown them a second living thing. That pheasant was the whole of the morning's catch for father and son, skin and bone, like hugging a mop. A pheasant was no deer hide. His father sat on a rock rubbing his knee and said nothing for a long time.

Just then dogs barked beyond the ridge, and seven or eight yellow hounds came pelting down the slope, with two Ma servants behind them, one shouldering a pitchfork, one carrying a gong. Leading the way at the very front was Liu Douya, old Liu's eldest boy, half an osmanthus cake clutched in his hand, cramming it into his mouth as he ran.

The one with the pitchfork was shouting from far off: "Stop! That pheasant's name is Ma!"

Xiaoman knew that half cake. When the two of them left the village before dawn, apart from Granny Wu at the east end, they had met only one person on the way: Liu Douya, crouched by the well gathering in his sparrow nets. The Mas' osmanthus cake is never given for nothing; this trip to the front hills had been bought with half a cake.

Xiaoman looked at the pheasant in his arms; it was skin and bone, and you couldn't tell what it was named. His father leaned on the bow and got up, but that leg wouldn't go fast. The barking came nearer. Xiaoman remembered his mother's words: if you can't win, run. But back the way they came were the Ma dogs; to either side were the Ma slopes.

There was only one direction the Ma dogs didn't go. He grabbed his father's arm. "Dad — further in."

Father and son limped off and pushed through a thicket of thorn; the yellow dogs chased them all the way to a broken stele — and there, all together, skidded to a stop, tails between their legs, whining, pawing at the ground, and would not take one step further.

The servant with the gong caught up, saw the stele, and went pale too. He grabbed the one with the pitchfork: "…Forget it. It's one pheasant." And lower: "That gentleman in white the other day — gave us two taels of silver, and this stone's the very thing he asked about. Even Third Master says keep our mouths shut." The one with the pitchfork glared at him, then shouted into the trees: "Third Master says anything shot in Black Pine Ridge before the Start of Winter is named Ma too!" The two of them called off the dogs and left without looking back.

Liu Douya trailed at the rear, glanced back at Xiaoman once, and swallowed the last mouthful of osmanthus cake.
